article.headline: Four Phases, Fifteen Years: A Road Map for the AI Investment Supercycle
article.lede: An anonymous X account named @cryptorand has published a widely shared infographic claiming the artificial-intelligence investment cycle will run fifteen years, divide into four identifiable phases, and already have its first behind it. The four-phase sequence — semiconductor makers, then data-centre infrastructure, then physical-world AI, then software dominance — maps closely enough onto institutional research to deserve analytical attention, even if its source carries no verifiable credentials. Reacting, a retail investor named @napoleon21st endorses the framework while promoting four small-cap names not on the original chart.
article.body:
The *AI supercycle* — a sustained, multi-decade capital wave driven by artificial-intelligence adoption — has accumulated credentialed backing. Raj Ganguly, co-CEO of venture firm B Capital Group, told CNBC in September 2025 that “it’s probably a 20-year super cycle,” bracketing the @cryptorand estimate of fifteen years within an institutional range. Goldman Sachs (GS) projects roughly $7.6 trillion in aggregate AI capital expenditure between 2026 and 2031, and IDC, the research firm, forecasts the semiconductor market alone will surpass $1.29 trillion in 2026 — a 52.8% single-year surge — using the supercycle label explicitly. Where the @cryptorand chart departs from institutional research is not in its duration claim but in its authority: the account is anonymous, carries no regulatory registration, and its framework synthesises circulating research themes rather than originating them.

The infographic’s more durable argument is its **phase-rotation thesis** — the claim that AI capital migrates in predictable sequence. Phase 1 (2023–2024) belonged to the semiconductor picks-and-shovels trade: Nvidia (NVDA) and Broadcom (AVGO) led it, and the chart correctly concedes that “most upside already [has been] captured.” Phase 2, framed as the present year, centres on the physical infrastructure of data centres — power generation, cooling, and high-speed networking. Phase 3 extends the AI stack into the physical world: rare earths, robotics, drones, and space. Phase 4 (2030 and beyond) arrives at software dominance and *AGI* infrastructure. Goldman Sachs has framed the current moment in nearly identical terms, and Global X ETFs publishes a three-stage thematic map that matches the first three phases almost exactly. Among the Phase 2 names on the @cryptorand chart, Vertiv (VRT) — maker of thermal and power-management systems for data centres — is the most institutionally validated: Q1 2026 revenue rose 30% year-over-year to $2.65 billion, with orders up 252%. Arista Networks (ANET), the dominant Ethernet-switching vendor for AI clusters, has raised its 2026 AI networking revenue target to $3.25 billion. GE Vernova (GEV) booked $2.4 billion in data-centre electrification orders in Q1 2026 alone.

What @napoleon21st adds is not drawn from the chart at all. The four tickers he promotes — Sivers Semiconductors (SIVE.ST), Silicom (SILC), LPKF Laser & Electronics (LPK.DE), and One Stop Systems (OSS) — appear nowhere in the infographic and represent his own Phase 2-to-3 small-cap overlay. Each has a specific technological rationale. Sivers manufactures the indium phosphide laser arrays at the core of *co-packaged optics* (CPO) — a technique for integrating optical transceivers directly onto AI chip packages, circumventing the copper-interconnect bottleneck that limits large-scale GPU cluster performance. Silicom makes FPGA-based *smart NICs* that handle packet processing and traffic steering independently of the host CPU at the data-centre network edge; Q1 2026 revenue rose 33% year-over-year and the company is co-developing an inference-specific NIC with a large AI compute customer for hyperscaler trials in the second half of 2026. LPKF’s proprietary LIDE process (*Laser-Induced Deep Etching*) drills the microscopic through-glass vias used in *glass core substrates* — advanced packaging components that route signals between chiplets and are Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing’s (TSM) declared scaling path beyond conventional silicon interposers. One Stop Systems builds ruggedised edge-computing servers for defence, aerospace, and autonomous systems; Q4 2025 revenue grew more than 70% year-over-year on defence programme wins including the P-8 Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft.

The phase-rotation thesis carries real execution and timing risk. Man Group (MAN.L), the listed alternative-asset manager, argues that the AI build-out suffers from a “closed-loop financing problem” — the largest technology companies acting simultaneously as suppliers, customers, investors, and validators, creating circular capital flows that may be partly divorced from verifiable end-market demand. Broadcom (AVGO) itself has publicly warned of an “AI digestion” period in which hyperscalers pause new hardware orders to integrate equipment already purchased, complicating the timing of any phase rotation. For napoleon21st’s small-cap picks the risks are more specific: Sivers (SIVE.ST) posted a SEK 186 million after-tax loss in 2025 and ran more than 1,200% year-to-date through early May 2026 on technology not yet in volume production; LPKF Laser & Electronics (LPK.DE) glass-substrate customers remain in test-and-R&D rollout; neither company’s shares trade on a US exchange. None of the four tickers carries multi-firm institutional analyst coverage of the kind attached to VRT, ANET, or GEV.

The bookmark is ultimately two things at once: an endorsement of a coherent, institutionally-aligned investment narrative with genuine analytical grounding, and a retail investor using that credible frame to promote four illiquid small-caps in which he appears to hold concentrated positions — none of which appeared in the framework he is citing. The pattern is familiar in financial social media: a persuasive macro scaffold lends authority to micro bets the author has already made. Whether SIVE, SILC, LPK, and OSS vindicate the thesis depends on engineering timelines, customer ramps, and market-access improvements that remain years from resolution.

concepts.definition: A prolonged, self-reinforcing wave of capital deployment driven by artificial-intelligence adoption, analogous in scope and duration to prior technology platform shifts such as electrification or the internet build-out. Analysts at B Capital, Sequoia Capital, and IDC use the term to describe a 15-to-20-year period of rising AI capital expenditure cascading across hardware, infrastructure, and software layers.

An investment thesis holding that capital migrates in sequence across distinct segments of a technology build-out — in the AI case, from semiconductor makers to data-centre infrastructure to physical-world AI applications and finally to software. Investors who correctly anticipate each rotation aim to own the next phase before it is widely recognised and priced in, accepting that early-phase winners may underperform once capital moves on.

A chip-packaging technique that integrates optical transceivers directly onto the same substrate as a processor or network switch, replacing copper wire for the shortest data links inside a server rack. CPO eliminates a key bandwidth and power bottleneck in large-scale AI GPU clusters and requires purpose-built laser light sources — such as the indium phosphide arrays that Sivers Semiconductors manufactures — positioned within millimetres of the chip die.

A network interface card equipped with an FPGA (field-programmable gate array) or a dedicated processor that handles packet processing, encryption, and traffic steering independently of the host CPU. Smart NICs accelerate data handling at the network edge of AI data centres and are increasingly used to offload the overhead of distributed inference workloads.

An advanced semiconductor packaging component made from ultra-thin glass, drilled with microscopic through-glass vias (TGVs) that carry electrical signals between chiplets assembled in a single package. Glass substrates offer lower signal loss and finer routing density than the organic laminates used in conventional chip packages, and are a declared scaling path at TSMC and Intel for the post-silicon-interposer era.

A proprietary laser-processing technique developed by LPKF Laser & Electronics for drilling high-aspect-ratio holes and precise structures in thin glass. LIDE is the manufacturing step that converts flat glass sheets into functional semiconductor substrates and interposers by creating the through-glass vias needed for electrical connectivity, and LPKF holds the key patents on the process.

A hypothetical class of AI systems capable of performing any intellectual task a human can accomplish, without domain-specific training. In investment discourse, AGI infrastructure is shorthand for the compute and energy capacity presumed necessary to train and operate such systems — used in the @cryptorand Phase 4 thesis to describe a long-dated bet on sustained demand for large-scale AI compute beyond narrow-purpose models.

article.fact_check: The quoted tweet body says “We’re in year 3,” but the infographic image explicitly labels the current moment “Year 4 of 15” and places Phase 2 in ‘Year 4.’ The discrepancy likely reflects the original tweet being written in late 2024 and the image being updated for 2025, but both elements appear in the same post, which is internally inconsistent. The 15-year supercycle duration is plausible but imprecise: credentialed institutional sources cite a 15-to-20-year range with no mathematical derivation for any specific figure.

ticker_nvda.name: NVIDIA Corporation
ticker_nvda.blurb: NVIDIA designs graphics processing units (GPUs) and system-on-chip products. Originally a gaming chip company, it became the dominant supplier of AI accelerators — chips that perform the parallel matrix math required to train and run large language models. Its H100, H200, and Blackwell GPU families are the de facto standard for AI training infrastructure at hyperscalers and cloud providers. NVIDIA's CUDA software ecosystem creates deep switching costs: virtually all AI frameworks and models are optimised for CUDA, making competing hardware difficult to adopt at scale. NVIDIA also sells networking (InfiniBand, Ethernet) and data-centre systems.
ticker_nvda.recent: NVIDIA reported FY2026 (ending Jan 2026) revenue of $215.9 billion, up 65% YoY, with data centre revenue reaching $186 billion. The company's forward P/E of ~17.5x on 34.8% projected EPS growth produces a PEG of 0.50 — unusually cheap for what is arguably the most critical infrastructure company in the AI buildout. Hyperscalers (Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta) collectively committed over $200 billion in AI infrastructure capex for 2026, the majority flowing through NVIDIA's supply chain.

ticker_avgo.name: Broadcom Inc.
ticker_avgo.blurb: Broadcom is a diversified semiconductor and infrastructure software company formed through a series of acquisitions, most recently VMware (closed 2023). Its chip portfolio spans networking ASICs (custom chips for hyperscaler AI clusters), enterprise storage controllers, WiFi silicon, and set-top-box processors. Broadcom's AI networking chips — particularly its Tomahawk Ethernet switching ASICs and custom AI accelerators built for Google, Meta, and Apple — have made it a second-tier AI infrastructure beneficiary behind NVIDIA. The VMware acquisition added high-margin enterprise software revenue that meaningfully improved the company's margin profile.
ticker_avgo.recent: Broadcom's FY2026 revenue (ending Oct 2026) is on track to exceed $65 billion, with AI-related chip revenue growing rapidly as hyperscalers expand custom silicon programs. Forward EPS growth of 56.3% and a forward P/E of ~23.4x produce a PEG of 0.42 — among the best risk-adjusted valuations in large-cap technology. CEO Hock Tan has guided to $60–90 billion in AI chip revenue by 2027 from three major hyperscaler customers alone.

ticker_gev.name: GE Vernova Inc.
ticker_gev.blurb: GE Vernova is the power and energy spinoff of General Electric, separated as an independent NYSE-listed company in April 2024. The company operates three segments: Power (gas turbines, steam turbines, grid services), Wind (onshore and offshore turbines), and Electrification (grid software, power conversion, high-voltage equipment). It is one of the few companies in the world capable of manufacturing heavy-duty gas turbines at scale, a competitive moat that has become highly significant as hyperscalers race to secure reliable power for AI data centres.
ticker_gev.recent: GE Vernova reported Q1 2026 revenue of $9.34 billion and net income of $4.75 billion, driven by record AI-linked orders. Its total backlog reached $150 billion — described by management as 'sold out for years.' The stock rose from its April 2024 IPO price of approximately $165 to $1,099 as of early May 2026, a gain of roughly 565%, making it one of the best-performing large-cap equities of the AI infrastructure cycle. Gas turbine lead times have stretched into the early 2030s, cementing GEV's pricing power. In 2025 full-year revenue was $38.1 billion (+9%), with net income of $4.9 billion, up 215% year-on-year. Analysts maintain a consensus Buy rating but the average 12-month price target of $1,068 implies the stock has largely priced in near-term upside.

ticker_silc.name: Silicom Ltd.
ticker_silc.blurb: Silicom is an Israeli supplier of high-performance networking hardware - smart NICs (network interface cards), FPGA-based accelerators, edge appliances and switch fabric components - sold mostly to OEMs that bake the boards into their own cybersecurity, SD-WAN, telecom and cloud-edge products. It is a classic small-cap design-win business: revenue depends on how many customer programs ramp into volume each year. Lod-headquartered, founded 1987.
ticker_silc.recent: Q1 2026 revenue of $19.1m was up 33% year-over-year and ahead of guidance; Q2 was guided to $20-21m and full-year 2026 to $82-83m. The balance sheet ended Q1 with no debt and about $109m of working capital and marketable securities ($63m cash and equivalents, $63m inventory). Management has banked four design wins in the first four months of 2026 against a target of seven to nine for the year, including a tier-one cybersecurity edge system worth over $1m of 2026 orders and an inference-specific NIC under co-development with one of two large AI compute customers, with hyperscaler proof-of-concept deployments slated for H2 2026.

ticker_tsm.name: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company
ticker_tsm.blurb: TSMC is the world's largest contract chipmaker, fabricating semiconductors designed by Nvidia, Apple, AMD, Qualcomm, and dozens of others. It controls roughly 60% of global foundry revenue and an even higher share of advanced-node manufacturing (3nm and below). TSMC's competitive position rests on process technology leadership, enormous capital expenditure scale, and a customer base that has no viable alternative at leading-edge geometries. Its Taiwanese concentration is the central geopolitical risk that market participants perpetually discount, then rediscover.
ticker_tsm.recent: TSMC reported Q1 2026 revenue of approximately NT$839 billion (roughly $26 billion USD), up around 41% year-over-year, driven by surging AI accelerator demand from Nvidia and Apple. The company's CoWoS advanced packaging capacity — critical for HBM memory integration in AI GPUs — remains sold out through at least 2026. TSMC appeared on Palantir's Q1 2026 Rule of 80 Frontier chart with a composite growth-plus-margin score of 88%, placing it fourth among large-cap companies on that metric.

poster_napoleon21st.blurb: Public information about @napoleon21st is thin. The X profile is login-walled to anonymous web fetches and the handle does not appear in indexed lists of small-cap or photonics commentators, in financial press citations, or in cached search results that would normally surface a high-engagement account. The post in question reads as that of an active retail investor with concentrated positions in three specialist semiconductor and photonics small-caps (SIVE, SILC, LPK) who is comfortable using LLM 'thinking models' as a sanity-check on his own theses.
poster_napoleon21st.credibility_note: No verifiable track record was located through public web search. Treat the account as an unfamiliar retail voice rather than an established analyst or fund manager. The post itself is candid - it labels the LLM output as 'not necessarily true' - which argues against treating it as a recommendation, but readers should not infer authority where the public record does not establish it.
